board_events.text: Degrees vs radians: whose ruler?
A degree is 1/360 of a full turn. Why 360? A Babylonian convention — nothing about a circle demands it.
A radian uses the circle itself: walk along the rim a distance equal to the radius, and the angle you sweep is 1 radian.

board_events.text: 1 radian ≈ 57.3° — a little less than 60°.
Radian = arc ÷ radius = length ÷ length, so it is a pure number with no units.
The whole rim is 2πr, i.e. 2π radius-lengths, so one full turn = $2\pi$ radians.
Anticlockwise rotation is a positive angle; clockwise is negative.
The cornerstone definition
Here $s$ is arc length and $r$ is radius. Both are lengths, so $\theta$ is dimensionless \u2014 a pure number.
Master conversion relation
Degree to radian: multiply by $\frac{\pi}{180}$. Radian to degree: multiply by $\frac{180}{\pi}$.
1° ≈ 0.01746 rad; 1 rad ≈ 57°16′. The two factors are reciprocals.
Standard angles: $30^\circ=\frac{\pi}{6}$, $45^\circ=\frac{\pi}{4}$, $60^\circ=\frac{\pi}{3}$, $90^\circ=\frac{\pi}{2}$, $180^\circ=\pi$, $360^\circ=2\pi$.
A bare number in this chapter always means radians.
From theta = s/r, everything follows
Proportion route: $\frac{s}{2\pi r}=\frac{\theta}{2\pi}$. The $2\pi$ cancels only because $\theta$ is in radians.
A sector is the same fraction of the disc as its angle is of the full turn: $\frac{A}{\pi r^2}=\frac{\theta}{2\pi}$.

segments.text: Let's begin the whole chapter with one honest question about angles.

You've always measured angles in degrees, but think about it: why exactly three hundred sixty parts in a full turn? The answer is just history. The Babylonians liked three hundred sixty because it divides so neatly. There is nothing about a circle that wants to be cut into that many pieces. A degree is a convention, like measuring cloth in cubits.

The radian throws away the invented number and lets the circle measure itself. Take any circle, walk along its edge a distance exactly equal to the radius, and the angle you've turned through, seen from the centre, is defined as one radian.
<curious>Here is that idea drawn out.</curious> The bent arc from A to B has the same length as the straight radius, and the angle it opens up at the centre O is precisely one radian.
Notice the size: one radian is about fifty seven point three degrees, a bit under sixty. Keep that picture, it's your sanity check for the whole chapter.

And here is the deep point. A radian is arc length divided by radius, that is, a length divided by a length. The units cancel completely, so a radian is a pure number. This is why later it can sit inside derivatives and power series where a degree never could.

Because the entire rim measures two pi radius-lengths, one complete turn is two pi radians. Half a turn is pi, a quarter turn is pi over two. The pi isn't decoration, it's literally how many radius-lengths wrap around the circle, halved.

One more convention we lock in now: rotating anticlockwise gives a positive angle, clockwise gives a negative one. An old clock's hands move clockwise, so by our rule they move in the negative direction.
Now the one definition everything else in this subtopic is built on.
The angle theta equals the arc length s divided by the radius r, with theta in radians. Memorise this single relation, not its consequences.

Look at the right side: s and r are both lengths, so their ratio has no dimension. That is the clean, formal reason a radian is a pure number, and it's the fact that quietly rescues you in Class twelve calculus.
From that definition comes the one relation you truly need for conversions.
Pi radians equal one hundred eighty degrees. Everything else is just scaling this.
To go from degrees to radians, multiply by pi over one hundred eighty. To go the other way, multiply by one hundred eighty over pi. Same relation, read in two directions.

<whisper>Two benchmarks worth burning in:</whisper> one degree is about zero point zero one seven radian, and one radian is about fifty seven degrees sixteen minutes. The two conversion factors are simply reciprocals of each other.
And lock the standard table cold: thirty is pi over six, forty five is pi over four, sixty is pi over three, ninety is pi over two, one hundred eighty is pi, three hundred sixty is two pi.
From here on, a bare number with no degree sign always means radians — no exceptions in this chapter.
Here is the payoff of that one definition: two famous formulas come out for free.
Rearrange theta equals s over r and you get arc length s equals r theta, with theta in radians.

The version examiners want is by proportion. Arc length is to the whole circumference as the angle is to the full turn: s over two pi r equals theta over two pi. The two pi cancels cleanly, and it only cancels because theta is in radians. In degrees you'd be stuck carrying an ugly pi over one eighty.
The sector area is just as easy. Area of a sector equals one half r squared theta.
The logic is identical: the sector is the same slice of the disc as its angle is of the whole turn, so area over pi r squared equals theta over two pi. Rearranged, that's one half r squared theta.
And a handy twin form, using s equals r theta, is area equals one half r times s.
This is the picture: two radii r, the arc s along the rim, the angle theta at the centre, and the shaded area.

<excited>Here's the warning that earns marks:</excited> all three formulas assume theta is in radians. Plug in degrees and your answer comes out about fifty seven times too big. Convert first, always.

board_events.text: Example 1 — convert 40°20′ to radians
Fold the minutes into degrees first: $40^\circ 20' = 40 + \tfrac{20}{60} = \tfrac{121}{3}$ degrees.
Example 2 — find the radius
A central angle of $60^\circ$ cuts an arc of $37.4$ cm. Convert first: $60^\circ=\frac{\pi}{3}$.
Signature trap: forgetting to turn 60° into radians before using s = rθ.
Example 3 — a spinning wheel
$360$ revolutions per minute $= \frac{360}{60}=6$ revolutions per second. Each revolution is $2\pi$.
This ω in rad s⁻¹ feeds straight into v = rω in rotational mechanics.
Example 4 — equal arcs in two circles
Same arc: $r_1\theta_1 = r_2\theta_2$. The angles appear only as a ratio, so degrees are fine here.
Bigger angle on the same arc means a smaller radius — the inverse relationship is the trap.
Example 5 — from chord to arc
Diameter $40$ cm gives $r=20$. A chord of $20$ cm; the perpendicular from the centre bisects it.
Example 6 — the sector inversion
Perimeter $2r+s=16$; area $\tfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta=16$, so $r^2\theta=32$ and $s=\tfrac{32}{r}$.
Two unknowns from two conditions — the JEE Advanced pattern: easy trig, hard algebra.
Traps in angle measurement
#1 Signature trap: using degrees inside s = rθ or A = ½ r²θ. Convert to radians first — always.
#2 Flipping the factor. Degree to radian uses π/180; radian to degree uses 180/π. They are reciprocals.
#3 A radian is dimensionless \u2014 don't 'cancel radians' like metres. In $\omega=\theta/t$ you simply get $\text{s}^{-1}$.
#4 DMS is base-60: 0.5° is 30′, not 50′; and 20′ is one-third of a degree.
#5 Clockwise is a negative angle. #6 Check your calculator's DEG vs RAD mode before numerical work.
Sanity check: 1 rad ≈ 57°. A huge 'radian' answer for a small angle means you flipped the factor.

segments.text: Let's put the conversion factor to work on a board-level problem.
We want forty degrees twenty minutes in radians. First deal with the minutes: twenty minutes is twenty over sixty of a degree, so the whole angle is one hundred twenty one over three degrees.

Now multiply by pi over one hundred eighty. One hundred twenty one over three, times pi over one hundred eighty, gives one hundred twenty one pi over five hundred forty radians. That's the answer, left symbolic in pi.
Second example, a classic find-the-radius problem.
A central angle of sixty degrees intercepts an arc of thirty seven point four centimetres. Before touching s equals r theta, convert: sixty degrees is pi over three radians.
Now r equals s over theta, which is thirty seven point four divided by pi over three. Using pi as twenty two over seven, this works out to thirty five point seven centimetres.
<whisper>Watch this one:</whisper> the single biggest mistake here is using sixty directly in s equals r theta without converting. Always send the angle to radians first.
This example is the quiet bridge from maths straight into physics.
A wheel makes three hundred sixty revolutions in a minute. Per second that's three hundred sixty over sixty, which is six revolutions. Each revolution is two pi radians.
So the angular speed omega is six times two pi, that is twelve pi, about thirty seven point seven radians per second.
That omega, in radians per second, is exactly what plugs into v equals r omega for rim speed. Fumble the units here and you lose marks in rotational mechanics too.
The fourth example is a favourite ratio trap.

Two circles have arcs of equal length subtending sixty degrees and seventy five degrees at their centres. Since the arcs are equal, r one theta one equals r two theta two. The angles only appear as a ratio, so we can leave them in degrees, the conversion factor would cancel anyway.
So r one over r two equals theta two over theta one, which is seventy five over sixty, equal to five over four.
Read the meaning: a bigger angle sitting on the same arc means a tighter, smaller circle. Students who memorised s equals r theta but never felt it often flip this and write four to five.
Example five chains two ideas: a chord relation, then the arc formula.

A circle of diameter forty gives radius twenty. A chord is twenty centimetres long. Drop a perpendicular from the centre; it bisects the chord, leaving a right triangle with hypotenuse twenty and half-chord ten.
So sine of theta over two equals ten over twenty, which is one half. That means theta over two is pi over six, so theta is pi over three.
Now the arc: s equals r theta, twenty times pi over three, which is twenty pi over three, about twenty point nine four centimetres.
Example six looks the hardest but the trig is trivial — it's an algebra puzzle in disguise.

A sector has perimeter sixteen and area sixteen. Perimeter is two radii plus the arc: two r plus s equals sixteen. Area is one half r squared theta equals sixteen, so r squared theta is thirty two, and since s equals r theta, s equals thirty two over r.

Substitute into the perimeter: two r plus thirty two over r equals sixteen. Clear it and you get r minus four, all squared, equals zero. So r is four, s is eight, and theta is s over r, which is two radians.
Notice the design: two unknowns pinned down by two conditions. The angle work is child's play; the difficulty is the algebra. That's the signature JEE Advanced move.
Before we leave radians, here are the traps that decide the easy marks.

The signature trap, number one: using degrees inside s equals r theta or the sector area formula. Both are defined for theta in radians. Convert first, every single time. A wrong answer about fifty seven times too large is the fingerprint of this error.
Number two, flipping the conversion factor. Degree to radian uses pi over one eighty; radian to degree uses one eighty over pi. They're reciprocals, so mixing them up scales your answer wildly.

Number three, treating radian as a unit you carry along. It's dimensionless. In omega equals theta over time, the radian vanishes and you're left with per-second. Don't cancel radians as if they were metres.

Number four, the base-sixty arithmetic of degrees, minutes, seconds. Half a degree is thirty minutes, not fifty. Twenty minutes is one third of a degree. Convert minutes and seconds to fractions before multiplying.
Number five, clockwise rotation is negative. And number six, when you start numerical trig, check whether your calculator is in degree or radian mode, wrong mode gives nonsense.
And the one-second sanity check to keep forever: one radian is about fifty seven degrees. If a small angle gives you a huge number of radians, you almost certainly flipped the factor.

board_events.text: Reciprocals always share their parent's sign.
The three Pythagorean identities
The first is just the circle equation $a^2+b^2=1$ with $a=\cos\theta,\ b=\sin\theta$. Divide by $\cos^2$ or $\sin^2$ for the others.
Ranges — the built-in sanity check
$\sin,\cos\in[-1,1]$; $\sec,\csc$ never lie strictly inside $(-1,1)$; $\tan,\cot$ sweep all reals.
A value outside its range is as impossible as negative mass. Range-check every answer.

segments.text: This subtopic is the single biggest upgrade in the chapter: from ratios to functions.

In earlier classes, sine, cosine and tangent were just side ratios in a right triangle, and a right triangle can only hold angles between zero and ninety degrees. But we want to talk about sine of two hundred ten degrees, or cosine of minus forty. For that we need a frame with no ninety-degree cap: the unit circle, a circle of radius one at the origin.
Here it is. Rotate a ray to angle theta, anticlockwise as we locked in earlier, and look at where its tip P lands, at coordinates a and b.
The whole engine is this: cosine of theta is the x-coordinate a, and sine of theta is the y-coordinate b.
Say it as a picture: cosine is how far across, sine is how far up. Every sign, every range, every quadrantal value comes straight out of that.

And because the point sits on a circle of radius one, it can never be more than one unit from the centre. So the size of sine is at most one, and the size of cosine is at most one, a physical fact becoming a mathematical range.
<curious>Hold on to this one sentence</curious> — cosine across, sine up — and the rest of the subtopic is just reading it off the picture.
Let's write the definitions for a point at any distance, not just radius one.
Take a point x, y on the terminal side, at distance r from the origin. Then sine is y over r, cosine is x over r, tangent is y over x.
Their reciprocals: cosecant is r over y, secant is r over x, cotangent is x over y.

Now the key observation. r is always positive, so it can never change a sign. The sign of every function is decided purely by the signs of x and y, that is, by the quadrant. That is the whole sign engine.
One pairing to fix now, because it trips people: cosecant pairs with sine, and secant pairs with cosine, despite the co in the name. Read the third letter. Co-sec-ant, the third letter matches sine.
The signs are captured by the classic mnemonic, All Silver Tea Cups.
In Quadrant one, all are positive. In two, sine and its reciprocal cosec. In three, tangent and cot. In four, cosine and sec.
Here it is on the circle, going anticlockwise, A, S, T, C.
<whisper>And remember,</whisper> a reciprocal always carries the same sign as its parent, so cosec follows sine, sec follows cosine.
Three identities power almost everything that follows.
First: sine squared plus cosine squared equals one.
Second: one plus tangent squared equals secant squared.
Third: one plus cotangent squared equals cosecant squared.

And you don't memorise them blind. The first is literally the circle's equation, a squared plus b squared equals one, with a as cosine and b as sine. Divide that through by cosine squared and you get the tangent-secant one; divide by sine squared and you get the cotangent-cosecant one. All three from one circle.
Now the layer that catches more mistakes than any other: ranges.

Sine and cosine live between minus one and one. Secant and cosecant, being reciprocals of things no bigger than one, can never sit strictly between minus one and one. Tangent and cotangent sweep every real number.
<excited>Treat this like dimensional analysis:</excited> a sine of one point two is as impossible as a negative mass. Make the range check the last thing you do on every problem.

$0^\circ$ and $90^\circ$ read straight off the circle: the points $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$.
Even and odd — the mirror across the x-axis
Replacing $\theta$ by $-\theta$ reflects the point across the $x$-axis: cosine (the $x$-coord) is unchanged, sine (the $y$-coord) flips.
One rule: '90° flips, 180° doesn't'
For $f(n\cdot 90^\circ \pm \theta)$: $n$ odd $\Rightarrow$ change to the co-function; $n$ even $\Rightarrow$ same function.
Sign: find the quadrant of the whole angle and apply ASTC to the original function.
Odd multiples of 90° sit on the vertical axis and swap sin ↔ cos.
Example 1 — sin 210°
Example 2 — cos(−300°)
Example 3 — sin 1230° (reduce first)
Example 4 — tan 135° (the co-function case)
Two routes agree: 135° = 180°−45° gives −tan 45° = −1 as well.
Example 5 — simplify to a constant
$\sin(90^\circ{+}\theta)=\cos\theta$; $\cos(180^\circ{-}\theta)=-\cos\theta$; $\cos(90^\circ{-}\theta)=\sin\theta$; $\sin(180^\circ{+}\theta)=-\sin\theta$.
Example 6 — prove cos(270°+θ) = sinθ
$270^\circ+\theta$ is in Quadrant IV (cosine $+$); $n=3$ is odd, so $\cos\to\sin$.

Long allied-angle products almost always collapse to ±1. If yours doesn't, recheck a sign.

#1 Signature trap: wrong sign in a reduction. The sign comes from the quadrant of the WHOLE allied angle via ASTC, applied to the original function.
#2 Forgetting to switch to the co-function at 90°/270°. Odd multiples flip sin ↔ cos; even multiples (180°, 360°) don't.

segments.text: The famous standard values aren't magic — they come from two triangles you already know.
Every so-called standard value is just a side ratio read off the forty five, forty five, ninety triangle, or the thirty, sixty, ninety triangle, and placed on the unit circle.

Here they are. On the left, an isosceles right triangle with legs one and one and hypotenuse root two. On the right, half an equilateral triangle: hypotenuse two, short side one, long side root three.
From the left triangle: sine forty five equals cosine forty five equals one over root two, and tangent forty five is one.
From the right triangle: sine thirty is one half, cosine thirty is root three over two, and sine sixty is root three over two.

<curious>Here's a lovely pattern to lock the sine row:</curious> for zero, thirty, forty five, sixty, ninety, sine is root zero over two, root one over two, root two over two, root three over two, root four over two. The cosine row is exactly that list, reversed.
And the two ends, zero and ninety, you just read off the circle: the point at zero is one comma zero, and at ninety it's zero comma one.
Two small ideas now let you evaluate essentially any angle.
First, even and odd. Replacing theta with minus theta reflects the point across the x-axis. The x-coordinate, cosine, is untouched; the y-coordinate, sine, flips sign.
So cosine of minus theta equals cosine theta, and secant is the same, these are even.
But sine of minus theta is minus sine theta, and tangent flips too, these are odd. Only cosine and secant are even; the other four are odd.
Second, the one rule that replaces the whole allied-angle table. To evaluate any function of n times ninety degrees, plus or minus theta.

Ask: is n odd or even? If n is odd, the ninety and two seventy cases, the function changes to its co-function, sine to cosine, tangent to cotangent. If n is even, the one eighty and three sixty cases, the function stays the same.
Then the sign: figure out which quadrant the whole angle lands in for small theta, and give the answer the sign the original function has there, straight from All Silver Tea Cups.
The reason odd flips: odd multiples of ninety sit on the vertical axis, and reflecting about a vertical direction swaps the roles of across and up, which is exactly swapping cosine and sine.
First up, sine of two hundred ten.
Write it as one eighty plus thirty; that lands in Quadrant three where sine is negative, and n equals two is even so the function stays sine. So it's minus sine thirty, minus one half.
Next, cosine of minus three hundred.
Cosine is even, so this equals cosine three hundred. Three hundred is three sixty minus sixty, Quadrant four, cosine positive, so it's plus cosine sixty, one half.
Third, sine of twelve thirty — and here you must reduce first.
Subtract three full turns, that's minus ten eighty, giving one fifty. One fifty is one eighty minus thirty, Quadrant two, sine positive, so sine thirty, one half.
Fourth, tangent of one thirty five, the co-function case.
Ninety plus forty five, n equals one is odd, so tangent becomes cotangent. It's in Quadrant two where tangent is negative, so minus cotangent forty five, which is minus one.

<whisper>Notice the cross-check:</whisper> you could instead write one thirty five as one eighty minus forty five, giving minus tangent forty five, also minus one. Two routes, same answer — that's your safety net.
Example five simplifies a four-term expression down to a single constant.

Reduce each piece: sine of ninety plus theta is cosine theta; cosine of one eighty minus theta is minus cosine theta; cosine of ninety minus theta is sine theta; sine of one eighty plus theta is minus sine theta.
Multiply and add: cosine times minus cosine, plus sine times minus sine, gives minus cosine squared minus sine squared, which is minus one. The whole expression collapses to a constant.
Example six is a short proof: show cosine of two seventy plus theta equals sine theta.
Two seventy plus theta sits in Quadrant four for small theta, where cosine is positive, and n equals three is odd so cosine becomes sine.
So the result is plus sine theta. Done.
Example seven is an intimidating-looking product and quotient of six reduced terms.
Reduce each term: the numerator becomes tangent squared theta while the denominator becomes minus tangent squared theta, so their ratio is simply minus one.
<excited>The lesson is worth gold:</excited> long allied-angle products almost always collapse to plus or minus one. If yours refuses to, you've dropped a sign — go back and find it.
Five traps to close out standard values and allied angles.

The signature trap: a wrong sign in a reduction. The sign is never guessed, it comes from the quadrant of the whole allied angle, read through All Silver Tea Cups, applied to the original function. Identify the quadrant first.
Second, forgetting to switch to the co-function at ninety or two seventy. Odd multiples of ninety flip sine and cosine; the even ones, one eighty and three sixty, leave the function alone.
Third, misremembering a standard value. Don't guess, rebuild it: sine row is root zero to root four, each over two, and cosine is that reversed.
Fourth, an even-odd slip. Only cosine and secant are even. Pulling a minus sign out of cosine of minus theta is simply wrong, cosine doesn't care about the sign of the angle.
Fifth, for angles above three sixty or below zero, subtract or add whole turns first, then apply the rule to what's left.

And a habit that saves you: most reductions have two routes, one thirty five as ninety plus forty five, or as one eighty minus forty five. Use whichever is faster, and let the other confirm your answer.

First up, sine of two hundred ten.
Write it as one eighty plus thirty; that lands in Quadrant three where sine is negative, and n equals two is even so the function stays sine. So it's minus sine thirty, minus one half.

Subtract three full turns, that's minus ten eighty, giving one fifty. One fifty is one eighty minus thirty, Quadrant two, sine positive, so sine thirty, one half.

Example five simplifies a four-term expression down to a single constant.

Reduce each piece: sine of ninety plus theta is cosine theta; cosine of one eighty minus theta is minus cosine theta; cosine of ninety minus theta is sine theta; sine of one eighty plus theta is minus sine theta.
Multiply and add: cosine times minus cosine, plus sine times minus sine, gives minus cosine squared minus sine squared, which is minus one. The whole expression collapses to a constant.
Example six is a short proof: show cosine of two seventy plus theta equals sine theta.
Two seventy plus theta sits in Quadrant four for small theta, where cosine is positive, and n equals three is odd so cosine becomes sine.
So the result is plus sine theta. Done.
Example seven is an intimidating-looking product and quotient of six reduced terms.
Reduce each term: the numerator becomes tangent squared theta while the denominator becomes minus tangent squared theta, so their ratio is simply minus one.
<excited>The lesson is worth gold:</excited> long allied-angle products almost always collapse to plus or minus one. If yours refuses to, you've dropped a sign — go back and find it.
Five traps to close out standard values and allied angles.

The signature trap: a wrong sign in a reduction. The sign is never guessed, it comes from the quadrant of the whole allied angle, read through All Silver Tea Cups, applied to the original function. Identify the quadrant first.
Second, forgetting to switch to the co-function at ninety or two seventy. Odd multiples of ninety flip sine and cosine; the even ones, one eighty and three sixty, leave the function alone.
Third, misremembering a standard value. Don't guess, rebuild it: sine row is root zero to root four, each over two, and cosine is that reversed.
Fourth, an even-odd slip. Only cosine and secant are even. Pulling a minus sign out of cosine of minus theta is simply wrong, cosine doesn't care about the sign of the angle.
Fifth, for angles above three sixty or below zero, subtract or add whole turns first, then apply the rule to what's left.

segments.text: A graph turns trigonometry from something you compute into something you can see.

Here's the trick: walk anticlockwise around the unit circle, and at each angle x plot your height, which is sine x, against the distance you've walked. That height, laid out along a line, is the sine wave.
This is it. The wave is literally the circle's up-coordinate, unrolled.

Follow the height: it rises to plus one at pi over two, drops back to zero at pi, dips to minus one at three pi over two, and returns to zero at two pi. Then a new lap begins and the whole shape repeats.
That repetition has a name, periodicity.
A function is periodic with period capital T if f of x plus T always equals f of x, and T is the smallest positive number that works.
Sine and cosine repeat every full turn, so their period is two pi. Tangent, though, repeats every half turn, its period is pi.
Why only pi for tangent? Tangent measures the direction of the line through the origin, and a line points the same way again after just one hundred eighty degrees.
One template covers every sine and cosine you'll meet: y equals a sine of b x plus c, all plus d.
The size of a stretches the wave vertically. That's the amplitude, how tall the peaks are.
The b squeezes it horizontally. A bigger b packs in more oscillations in the same space, which means a shorter period.
See it here: compared to plain sine x, the red curve two sine x is twice as tall, and the green curve sine two x oscillates twice as fast.
The c slides the wave sideways, a phase shift, and d lifts the whole wave up or down.
So amplitude is the size of a, period is two pi over the size of b, and the vertical shift is d.
And crucially, the range becomes d minus the size of a, up to d plus the size of a. The shift d moves the entire band, don't forget it.
Here is the full reference you need to read or sketch any trig graph.
Base periods: sine, cosine, secant and cosecant all repeat over two pi; tangent and cotangent repeat over pi.
The scaling rule: the period of a function of b x plus c is the base period divided by the size of b. The constant c only shifts the graph, it never changes the period.
Here's the tangent graph to fix those ideas: period pi between branches, with vertical asymptotes at the odd multiples of pi over two, wherever cosine is zero.
Now the composites that trip students.

The absolute values of sine and cosine, and sine squared and cosine squared, all have period pi, not two pi. And for a sum of functions, the period is the least common multiple of the individual periods.
For asymptotes: tangent and secant blow up where cosine is zero, the odd multiples of pi over two; cotangent and cosecant blow up where sine is zero, the whole multiples of pi.

And the master transform line: for a sine of b x plus c, all plus d, amplitude is the size of a, period is two pi over the size of b, phase shift is minus c over b, and range is d minus the size of a to d plus the size of a.

board_events.text: Example 1 — read off three periods
Example 2 — range and period of 3 + 2 sin x
Amplitude $2$, vertical shift $3$: range $=[3-2,\,3+2]=[1,5]$. The $\sin x$ is unscaled, so period $2\pi$.
Example 3 — amplitude and period of −4 cos(x/3)
The minus flips the graph vertically but changes neither amplitude nor period.
Example 4 — period of |sin x| + |cos x|
Each of $|\sin x|,|\cos x|$ has period $\pi$. But $|\cos x|=|\sin(x+\tfrac{\pi}{2})|$, so the sum repeats sooner.
A hidden shrink: the sum's period is smaller than either part. Don't just take the larger.
Example 5 — period of sin²x
So $\sin^2 x$ has period $\pi$, not $2\pi$ \u2014 squaring halves the period here.
Example 6 — how many solutions of |sin x| = |cos x| in [0, 2π]?
$|\sin x|=|\cos x| \iff |\tan x|=1$, the four points where the two 'tent' graphs cross.
Example 7 — solve sin x ≥ 1/2 on [0, 2π]
Draw the line $y=\tfrac12$ and shade where the sine curve sits on or above it, between its two crossings.
General solution: x ∈ [2nπ + π/6, 2nπ + 5π/6], n an integer.
Graph and period traps
#1 Signature trap: multiplying instead of dividing for the period. sin(bx) has period 2π/|b|, not 2π·b. Bigger b means shorter period.
#2 Using $2\pi$ for tangent. $\tan$ and $\cot$ have base period $\pi$.
#3 Period of a sum is the LCM of the parts — and watch for a hidden shrink, as in |sin x| + |cos x|.
#4 Forgetting the vertical shift in the range. Range of $a\sin x + d$ is $[d-|a|,\,d+|a|]$, not $[-|a|,|a|]$.
#5 Swapping asymptotes: $\tan,\sec$ blow up at odd $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$; $\cot,\csc$ at $n\pi$. #6 Decide open vs closed endpoints by whether the inequality is strict.
Golden rule: divide (don't multiply) for period; tangent's period is π.

segments.text: Three quick reads to make the scaling rule automatic.

For the periods: sine three x divides two pi by three, giving two pi over three. Tangent two x uses the tangent base pi over two, so pi over two. And cosine of x over two divides two pi by one half, which is four pi, a stretched, slower wave.
Second, the range and period of three plus two sine x.
The amplitude is two and the vertical shift is three, so the range is three minus two to three plus two, that is one to five. The x inside sine is unscaled, so the period is just two pi.
Third, the amplitude and period of minus four cosine of x over three.
Amplitude is the size of minus four, which is four. Period is two pi over one third, which is six pi.
Notice the minus sign flips the graph upside down, but it touches neither the amplitude nor the period, both come from sizes only.
These two show that periods can shrink in ways you must watch for.

Take the absolute value of sine x plus the absolute value of cosine x. Each absolute value on its own has period pi. But the absolute value of cosine x is the same as the absolute value of sine of x plus pi over two, so the two swap roles.
Push x forward by pi over two and the sum returns to itself: it becomes absolute cosine plus absolute sine, exactly f of x again. No smaller shift works, so the period is pi over two.
This is a hidden shrink. The sum repeats faster than either piece alone, so never just take the larger of the two periods, check carefully.
Example five: the period of sine squared x.
Use the power-reduction identity: sine squared x equals one minus cosine two x, all over two. The only moving part is cosine two x, which has period two pi over two, that is pi.
So sine squared x has period pi, not two pi. Squaring the sine has quietly halved its period.
Graphs are the fastest way to count solutions and solve inequalities.
How many x in zero to two pi satisfy absolute sine equals absolute cosine? Divide through and it becomes the absolute value of tangent equals one, the points where the two tent-shaped graphs cross.
Those are pi over four, three pi over four, five pi over four, and seven pi over four, four solutions in one lap.
Example seven, an inequality: solve sine x at least one half on zero to two pi.
Draw the horizontal line y equals one half, and shade every place the sine curve sits on or above it. That's the stretch between its two crossing points.
Reading it off, x runs from pi over six to five pi over six, inclusive.
And by periodicity the general answer repeats every full turn: x lies between two n pi plus pi over six and two n pi plus five pi over six, for any integer n.
Six traps that decide the graph and period marks.
The signature trap: multiplying when you should divide. Sine of b x has period two pi over the size of b, not two pi times b. A bigger b means a shorter period, more waves squeezed in.
Second, using two pi for tangent. Tangent and cotangent have base period pi, half of the others.
Third, the period of a sum is the least common multiple of the parts, and stay alert for a hidden shrink like absolute sine plus absolute cosine, which drops all the way to pi over two.
Fourth, forgetting the vertical shift in the range. The range of a sine x plus d is d minus the size of a to d plus the size of a, not simply minus the size of a to the size of a.

Fifth, swapping asymptote locations. Tangent and secant blow up at the odd multiples of pi over two; cotangent and cosecant at the whole multiples of pi. And sixth, decide open versus closed endpoints by whether the inequality is strict.
The golden rule to carry: divide, never multiply, when finding a period, and remember tangent's period is pi.

segments.text: This subtopic looks like a forest of formulas, so let me hand you the one seed they all grow from.
Sum, difference, double, half, triple, product-to-sum, sum-to-product, every one of them is the same idea in a different costume.
The master key is the cosine difference formula: cosine of A minus B equals cosine A cosine B plus sine A sine B. Burn this one in.
Here's the family tree. Everything you'll ever need in this subtopic hangs off that single root at the top.
Watch how they grow. Replace B with minus B and you get cosine of A plus B. Use the cofunction shift, sine equals cosine of ninety minus the angle, and out fall sine of A plus or minus B.
Set B equal to A and you get the double-angle formulas. Halve the angle for half-angle. Add and subtract pairs and you get product-to-sum. One idea, eight costumes.
So the instruction is: don't memorise the list, learn the derivation. Under exam pressure you can rebuild any of them from cosine of A minus B in about twenty seconds, and it never fails you.
Before the catalogue, let's be clear what a compound angle even is, and what it is not.
It's just an angle built from two others, A plus B or A minus B. And the tempting guess, that sine of A plus B equals sine A plus sine B, is simply false.
Test it: let A and B both be thirty degrees. Sine of sixty is root three over two, about zero point eight seven. But sine thirty plus sine thirty is one half plus one half, which is one. Not equal.
The lesson is deep: trig functions are not linear, they never distribute over a sum. Kill this instinct early and you avoid the most common error in the whole chapter.
Here's the intuition for the amplitude form, which we'll lean on.
Push a swing partly sideways, a cosine x, and partly forward, b sine x. The two combine into one single push, of strength R, in one combined direction.
That is, a cosine x plus b sine x equals R cosine of x minus alpha, where R is the square root of a squared plus b squared.
And because a cosine ranges between plus and minus one, the maximum of the whole thing is plus R and the minimum is minus R, no calculus required.
Here's the first block of the catalogue, the sum and difference formulas.
For cosine of A plus or minus B: cosine A cosine B, then minus or plus sine A sine B. The sign is opposite to the one inside.
For sine of A plus or minus B: sine A cosine B, then plus or minus cosine A sine B. The sign matches the one inside.
For tangent of A plus or minus B: tangent A plus or minus tangent B, all over one minus or plus tangent A tangent B.
One clean mnemonic ties them: cosine flips the sign, sine follows the sign, and for tangent the denominator's sign is opposite the numerator's.

And this is where the master formula comes from, geometrically: two equal chords on the unit circle, one spanning A to B and one spanning A minus B back to the point one, zero. Equal central angles force equal chords, and equating their squared lengths gives cosine of A minus B.
Two products worth memorising.
Cosine of A plus B times cosine of A minus B equals cosine squared A minus sine squared B.
And sine of A plus B times sine of A minus B equals sine squared A minus sine squared B.
Set B equal to A in the sum formulas and the double-angle family drops out.
Sine two A is two sine A cosine A, and tangent two A is two tangent A over one minus tangent squared A.
Cosine two A has three faces: cosine squared A minus sine squared A, or two cosine squared A minus one, or one minus two sine squared A. Choose whichever matches what you're given.
Rearranging cosine two A gives the half-angle, or power-reduction, forms.
One plus cosine A is two cosine squared of A over two; one minus cosine A is two sine squared of A over two, the workhorses for integrals later.
Next, the t-substitution, with t as tangent of A over two.

It turns any rational trig expression into a rational function of t: sine A is two t over one plus t squared, cosine A is one minus t squared over one plus t squared, tangent A is two t over one minus t squared.
And the triple-angle pair, built from three A equals two A plus A.
Sine three A is three sine A minus four sine cubed A, and cosine three A is four cosine cubed A minus three cosine A.
The last formula block: turning products into sums and back, plus two headline results.

Product to sum: twice sine A cosine B is sine of A plus B plus sine of A minus B; twice cosine A cosine B is cosine of A plus B plus cosine of A minus B. The leading two is part of the formula, never drop it.
And twice sine A sine B is cosine of A minus B minus cosine of A plus B.
Now run it backwards, sum to product.
Sine C plus sine D is two sine of the half-sum times cosine of the half-difference; cosine C plus cosine D is two cosine of the half-sum times cosine of the half-difference.
The one to watch: cosine C minus cosine D carries a leading minus, it's minus two sine of the half-sum times sine of the half-difference.

Now substitute cosine squared B as one minus sine squared B, and sine squared A as one minus cosine squared A. Expand and everything cancels down to cosine squared A minus sine squared B. Proved.
Third, sine of seven pi over twelve.

Now sine of A plus B is sine A cosine B plus cosine A sine B: three fifths times minus twelve thirteenths, plus four fifths times five thirteenths. That's minus thirty six plus twenty, over sixty five, giving minus sixteen over sixty five.

board_events.text: Two layers of answer
A principal solution lies in $[0,2\pi)$. For $\sin\theta=\tfrac12$ there are two: $\tfrac{\pi}{6}$ and $\tfrac{5\pi}{6}$.
Like a train timetable: not one arrival time, but the whole recurring schedule, with n counting the laps.
The job is never to find a solution — it is to describe every solution in one stroke.
Losing roots by dividing
If you cancel $\cos\theta$ from $\sin\theta\cos\theta=\cos\theta$, you silently throw away every solution where $\cos\theta=0$.
Cancelling assumes the thing you cancel is non-zero — but here it can be zero. Factor, never divide.
Gaining roots by squaring
Squaring both sides can make a false equation look true, since $(-1)^2=1^2$.

Example 1 — principal solutions of sin x = 1/2
Example 2 — general solution of cos x = −1/2
Example 3 — quadratic in sin x: 2sin²x + sinx − 1 = 0
Factor as $(2\sin x - 1)(\sin x + 1)=0$, so $\sin x=\tfrac12$ or $\sin x=-1$.
Example 4 — solve √3 cos x + sin x = 1
$R=\sqrt{3+1}=2$, $\tan\alpha=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}\Rightarrow\alpha=\tfrac{\pi}{6}$. So $\cos(x-\tfrac{\pi}{6})=\tfrac12=\cos\tfrac{\pi}{3}$.
Example 5 — factor, don't divide: sin 2x = sin x
$\sin x = 0 \Rightarrow x=n\pi$; $\cos x=\tfrac12 \Rightarrow x=2n\pi\pm\tfrac{\pi}{3}$.
Dividing by sin x would erase the entire x = nπ family — the signature trap.
Example 6 — solve sin x + cos x = 1 (without squaring)
Amplitude form: $\sin x+\cos x=\sqrt2\,\sin(x+\tfrac{\pi}{4})$, so $\sin(x+\tfrac{\pi}{4})=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}=\sin\tfrac{\pi}{4}$.
Squaring instead gives sin 2x = 0, which admits x = π — but sinπ + cosπ = −1. Back-checking removes it.
Example 7 — range squeeze: 2sin²x + sin²2x = 2
With $\sin^2 2x = 4\sin^2 x\cos^2 x$ and $s=\sin^2 x$: $2s+4s(1-s)=2 \Rightarrow (2s-1)(s-1)=0$.
Equation traps
#1 Signature trap: dividing by a trig factor and losing roots. Never cancel sin x or cos x — factor and set each factor to zero.
#2 Squaring and keeping extraneous roots. Every candidate from a squared step must be checked in the original equation.
#3 Mixing the families. Sine: $n\pi+(-1)^n\alpha$; cosine: $2n\pi\pm\alpha$; tangent: $n\pi+\alpha$. Never borrow another's form.
#4 Giving only principal solutions when 'general' is asked — the integer n is mandatory.
#5 Ignoring solvability: if $|c|>\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$, declare 'no solution'. #6 Drop roots where tan, sec, cot or csc is undefined.
Golden rules: factor (never divide); back-check after squaring; keep the n; match the right family.

segments.text: A trig equation asks: for which angles does this statement hold? And the answer is almost never a single number.
Because trig functions repeat forever, if one angle solves sine theta equals one half, then adding any whole number of full turns gives another solution, and so does that angle's mirror partner.
See it on the circle: the line y equals one half cuts the sine at two places in the first lap, at pi over six and five pi over six, and each of those repeats every two pi.
So think in two layers.
A principal solution lives in the first lap, zero up to two pi. For sine theta equals one half there are exactly two: pi over six and five pi over six.
The general solution packages every answer with an integer n: theta equals n pi plus minus one to the n, times pi over six.
It's exactly a train timetable. You don't answer when is a train here with one time, you give the recurring schedule, and n counts the laps.
So the real job is never just to find a solution, it's to describe all of them in a single formula.
Two dangers cause almost every wrong answer in this subtopic, and both are conceptual.
The first is losing roots by dividing. Suppose you have sine theta cosine theta equals cosine theta, and you cancel cosine theta from both sides.
The moment you cancel, you silently throw away every solution where cosine theta is zero.
Cancelling secretly assumes the thing you cancel is non-zero. But here it can be zero, that's exactly the case you just deleted. So factor, and set each factor to zero, never divide.
The second danger is gaining roots by squaring. Squaring both sides can make a false statement look true, because minus one squared equals one squared.

Watch: sine x plus cosine x equals one. Square it and you get sine two x equals zero, which includes x equal to pi. But sine pi plus cosine pi is minus one, not one, so x equal to pi is a fake, an extraneous root.
So every candidate that comes out of a squared equation must be checked back in the original, and the fakes discarded.
These are the two signature traps of the whole subtopic, and notice, they're gaps in understanding, not careless arithmetic.
Here is the short, fixed list that solves the whole subtopic. Start with the zero cases.
Sine theta is zero at whole multiples of pi; cosine theta at odd multiples of pi over two; tangent theta at whole multiples of pi.
Now the three master general solutions, one per function.
For sine theta equals sine alpha: theta is n pi plus minus one to the n, times alpha.
For cosine theta equals cosine alpha: theta is two n pi plus or minus alpha; and for tangent theta equals tangent alpha: theta is n pi plus alpha. Never borrow another function's form.
One more covers all squared cases: sine squared, cosine squared, or tangent squared equal to the same of alpha gives theta equals n pi plus or minus alpha.
Then the linear form and its solvability test.

Rewrite a cosine theta plus b sine theta as R cosine of theta minus alpha equals c; it's solvable only if the size of c is at most the square root of a squared plus b squared, otherwise there is no solution.

And run the root-validity checklist every time: keep the integer n, restore any roots lost to division, back-check every candidate after squaring, and drop any out-of-domain root. Throughout, n is an integer.
Three foundational solves.

First, principal solutions of sine x equals one half. Sine is positive in the first and second quadrants, so within one lap we get x equals pi over six, and x equals pi minus pi over six, which is five pi over six.
Second, the general solution of cosine x equals minus one half. Minus one half is cosine of two pi over three, so by the cosine formula, x equals two n pi plus or minus two pi over three.
Third, a quadratic in sine x: two sine squared x plus sine x minus one equals zero.
Treat sine x as the variable and factor: two sine x minus one, times sine x plus one, equals zero. So sine x is one half, or sine x is minus one.
From sine x equals one half, x is n pi plus minus one to the n times pi over six. From sine x equals minus one, x is four n minus one, times pi over two.

Rewrite as two cosine of x minus pi over six equals one, that is cosine of x minus pi over six equals one half, which is cosine pi over three.

So x minus pi over six equals two n pi plus or minus pi over three, giving x equals two n pi plus pi over two, or x equals two n pi minus pi over six. And the size of c, one, is at most R, two, so solutions do exist.

Write sine squared two x as four sine squared x cosine squared x, and let s be sine squared x. Then two s plus four s times one minus s equals two, which tidies to two s minus one, times s minus one, equals zero.

board_events.text: Fast-recall golden rules
Angles: any arc / sector / calculus formula assumes radians. Convert first, always.
Functions: magnitude from the identity, sign from the quadrant — always two steps. Range-check every answer.
Allied angles: odd multiple of 90° ⇒ swap to co-function; sign from the quadrant via ASTC.
Graphs: divide (don't multiply) for the period; tangent's period is π; include the vertical shift in the range.
Identities: reconstruct everything from cos(A−B); watch every ±; amplitude is √(a²+b²), never a+b.
Equations: factor (never divide); back-check after squaring; keep the n; match the right solution family.
If a final sin or cos exceeds 1 in magnitude, or a period looks multiplied not divided — stop and recheck.
